question: What share of ICSID's in-person hearings in fiscal 2026 took place at the World Bank Group Paris Conference Centre and partner facilities?
answer: In fiscal 2026, 30 percent of all in-person hearings took place at the World Bank Group Paris Conference Centre and partner facilities [wbg-ar-2026:p43:para:002].

events.query: ICSID in-person hearings fiscal 2026 World Bank Group Paris Conference Centre partner facilities share percentage

results.text:
The Paris Office, announced in March 2026 and to
be located at the World Bank Group’s Paris office,
will support training activities and strengthen
connections with State officials, legal practitioners, and
organizations in the region and beyond. Paris has long
been one of the Centre’s most active hearing venues.
In fiscal 2026, 30 percent of all in-person hearings were
held at the World Bank Group Paris Conference Centre,
ICSID’s premier hearing venue in use since 1972, and
at facilities of leading institutions with which ICSID has
established cooperation agreements.
Together, these offices reflect ICSID’s commitment to
bringing its services closer to Member States, parties,
and practitioners.
SHARING KNOWLEDGE, SUPPORTING
PRACTITIONERS AND POLICYMAKERS
As part of the Knowledge Bank, ICSID produces and
shares knowledge that actively contributes to the
development and modernization of international
investment law and dispute settlement.

Of all
the in-person hearings in fiscal 2026, 44 percent were
held at ICSID’s hearing center in Washington, D.C., with
the remainder taking place at venues agreed upon by
the parties: Paris (30 percent), London (12 percent),
Singapore (5 percent), and other locations (9 percent).
ICSID continued to see a diverse pool of arbitrators,
conciliators, and committee members in fiscal 2026.
The Centre recorded 250 appointments to ICSID
cases, the second highest number in a single fiscal
year. Appointees represented 52 different nationalities,
and 29 percent of all appointments were nationals from
low- or middle-income economies. First-time appointees
accounted for 8 percent of all appointments; among
them, 25 percent were nationals of low- or middleincome economies and 35 percent were women.
The ICSID Secretariat comprises 76 staff members representing 39 nationalities and
speaking 22 languages, providing professional legal, administrative, and financial
services across all cases.

EXPANDING GLOBAL PRESENCE
ICSID has long maintained a broad international reach,
and expanding its global presence is among its current
institutional priorities. Fiscal 2026 marked a landmark
moment in this effort with the announcement of new
offices in Singapore and Paris, the Centre’s first staffed
offices outside Washington, D.C. This expansion will
enhance ICSID’s capacity to deliver tailored support,
strengthen outreach, and maintain the highest
standards in case management.
The Singapore office, announced in August 2025, is
located at the World Bank Group’s Singapore office and
at Maxwell Chambers. It will serve as a regional hub

question: What employment impact is expected from the World Bank's multi-country health operation in the Pacific?
answer: The World Bank's multi-country health operation in the Pacific (the Pacific Healthy Islands Transformation project) is expected to safeguard 16,000 health and health-support jobs across the Pacific through its financing, and it is also set to help Pacific Island countries establish the fundamental conditions for jobs and growth [wbg-ar-2026:p12:para:002].

supports our strategic priority of delivering quality, affordable health services to

Development Bank under the Full Mutual Reliance Framework, helping reduce
transaction costs. The OPEC Fund and the Pandemic Fund are also co-financing
PHIT, which is set to help Pacific Island countries establish the fundamental

Pacific Island countries face some of the world’s highest rates of premature death and
disability from non-communicable disease, including diabetes, cardiovascular disease,
and cancer, alongside persistent communicable diseases. Local healthcare systems
struggle to provide care to dispersed populations, and the resulting inefficiencies drive
up service costs and hamper job creation and long-term growth.
The World Bank’s Pacific Healthy Islands Transformation (PHIT) project, approved in
fiscal 2026, is taking a new approach to improving the health of people across the
region. The $239.5 million project covers Fiji, Kiribati, Tonga, and Tuvalu, and — through
the Pacific Community — Naoero, Samoa, Solomon Islands, and Vanuatu.

Leveraging the expertise of Knowledge Bank teams at the World Bank and IFC, PHIT will
create, protect, and safeguard 16,000 vital health and health-support jobs across the
Pacific — spanning frontline service delivery, infrastructure development, digital health
systems, supply chains, and monitoring and evaluation — representing a major
investment in the region’s most critical asset: its people. AI-enabled diagnostics and
regional telehealth networks will enable more patients to receive accurate diagnostics;
expanded access to specialized services, including regional radiotherapy and advanced
medical imaging, will serve patients with specific needs. Together, these advancements
will accelerate regional health and development impact for greater resilience,
productivity, and inclusive growth.

question: How long do contract-based arbitrations at ICSID take on average compared with the overall caseload?
answer: Contract-based arbitrations at ICSID are more time-efficient than the overall caseload, averaging 40 months from registration to conclusion compared to 47 months for the overall caseload [wbg-ar-2026:p43:para:003].

events.query: contract-based arbitrations at ICSID take on average compared with the overall caseload

results.text:
In fiscal 2026, ICSID published its first in-depth study on
contract-based investment dispute resolution, drawing
on an analysis of 175 cases registered under the ICSID
Convention and Additional Facility. The background
paper examines how contract-based dispute resolution
has worked in practice at ICSID, serving as both an
analytical guide and practical reference for investors,
States, and State entities. Key findings show that
contract-based arbitrations at ICSID are more timeefficient than the overall caseload, averaging 40 months
from registration to conclusion compared to 47, and
settle or discontinue at a higher rate, 43 percent versus
34 percent. The paper is accompanied by a special
issue of the ICSID Caseload – Statistics featuring data on
contract-based cases.

Two issues of the ICSID Caseload – Statistics were also
released. Published every six months in English, French,
and Spanish, this publication offers a comprehensive,
data-driven overview of all cases registered and
administered by ICSID since 1972, serving as a key
resource for practitioners and policymakers to track
trends and developments in international investment
dispute settlement.
Visit icsid.worldbank.org/resources/
publications to download and read all ICSID
publications.
CASE MANAGEMENT AND
DISPUTE RESOLUTION
ICSID administers investment disputes arising from
contracts, treaties, or laws when agreed upon by the
parties involved. Disputes are decided by an arbitral
tribunal or a conciliation commission, whose members
are typically appointed by the parties from among
international jurists worldwide. The Centre also offers
mediation and fact-finding procedures, and provides
administrative services for arbitrations conducted
under UNCITRAL and other non-ICSID frameworks.

Of the arbitrations concluded in fiscal 2026, 63 percent
were decided by a tribunal and 37 percent were settled
or otherwise discontinued, broadly reflecting ICSID’s
long-term trend of arbitration outcomes. Among
disputes decided by tribunals in the past year,
37 percent of awards upheld claims in part or in full,
40 percent rejected all claims on the merits, 18 percent
declined jurisdiction, and 5 percent of cases were
dismissed for manifest lack of legal merit.

question: Which country was the first to receive a 43-year IBRD loan under the Framework for Financial Incentives, and how does that tenor compare with the standard one?
answer: Tunisia was the first country to receive a 43-year IBRD loan under the Framework for Financial Incentives [wbg-ar-2026:p19:para:008]. This tenor is eight years longer than the current standard tenor of 35 years [wbg-ar-2026:p19:para:008].

events.query: 43-year IBRD loan Framework for Financial Incentives first country tenor standard

results.text:
DELIVERING MORE FOR CLIENTS
Further promoting private capital mobilization, we
helped countries refinance their outstanding IBRD
loans on now-proven projects where lending can be
considered “de-risked” from a commercial lender’s
perspective. For India, this approach unlocked nearly
$1.5 billion in new borrowing capacity from IBRD.
We advanced the Framework for Financial Incentives,
which offers volume, tenor, and price incentives, to
encourage clients to undertake projects that address
global challenges with cross-border benefits. Under
the framework, Tunisia became the first country
benefiting from a 43-year IBRD loan, eight years
more than the current 35 years, and received
$150 million beyond the country allocation by
signing a $430 million financing package to
support energy sector modernization.

AND FINANCIAL MODEL
IBRD finances its loans through its own equity and by
borrowing in the capital markets via the issuance of
IBRD bonds to fund development projects in member
countries. IBRD is rated triple-A by both Moody’s and
Standard & Poor’s, and investors view its bonds as highquality and liquid securities. IBRD’s funding approach
continues to aim to achieve the best long-term value
for borrowing members on a sustainable basis. IBRD’s
ability to channel the funds it raises in international
capital markets to developing member countries is
important in achieving its goals.
IBRD’s approach has enabled it to borrow at favorable
market terms and pass the savings on to its borrowing
members. Funds not immediately deployed for lending
are held in IBRD’s investment portfolio to provide
liquidity for its operations. In fiscal 2026, IBRD raised
nearly $50 billion by issuing medium- and long-term
bonds in a variety of currencies.

MAXIMIZE DEVELOPMENT IMPACT
Shareholder support for IBRD’s innovative financing
instruments continued to grow in fiscal 2026,
strengthening our capacity to scale lending and tackle
global challenges. Singapore pledged funds to our
hybrid capital instrument and New Zealand became
the first shareholder to subscribe to our Enhanced
Callable Capital instrument, bringing hybrid capital
contributions to $1.2 billion. Together, these new
instruments demonstrate IBRD’s strong leveraging
power, turning $1 into $6-10 of additional lending over
time, and unlocking tens of billions for global impact.
IBRD has continued to structure outcome bonds that mobilize private capital for
specific development projects. For example, in December 2025, IBRD issued a
$200 million principal-protected bond, the Clean Cooking Outcome Bond, that
mobilized private capital to support the distribution and use of cleaner cooking
stoves in Ghana.

question: What financial commitment did Norway make when it joined MIGA's West Bank and Gaza trust fund as a donor?
answer: When Norway joined MIGA's West Bank and Gaza Investment Guarantee Trust Fund as a donor, it pledged approximately $5 million over five years [wbg-ar-2026:p41:para:001].

events.query: Norway financial commitment MIGA West Bank Gaza trust fund donor

results.text:
GUARANTEE TRUST FUND
A notable milestone during this reporting period was
the Kingdom of Norway’s decision to join MIGA’s West
Bank and Gaza Investment Guarantee Trust Fund as a
new donor, pledging approximately $5 million over five
years. This contribution, formalized on the sidelines
of the 2025 World Bank Group–IMF Annual Meetings,
marks the first expansion of the donor base since
the trust fund’s establishment in 1997 and reflects
growing international confidence in MIGA’s ability
to operate in highly fragile environments. Norway’s
support will strengthen the fund’s capacity to provide
political risk insurance, and trade finance guarantees
in collaboration with IFC and the European Bank for
Reconstruction and Development and mobilize private
investment in the West Bank and Gaza, where elevated
risks have historically constrained capital flows. This will
help sustain economic activity, support job creation,
and advance recovery and reconstruction efforts.
MIGA EXPANDS GLOBAL

THROUGH GUARANTEES
The government of Japan and MIGA deepened a
long-standing partnership to scale up the mobilization
of private capital in developing countries. Japan
committed nearly $20 million in additional funding to
MIGA-administered trust funds, reinforcing its position
as a leading contributor and strategic partner. This
support will expand MIGA’s ability to deploy political
risk insurance and trade finance guarantees in fragile
and conflict-affected situations — including Ukraine and
the West Bank and Gaza — as well as to advance energy
transition projects in emerging and frontier markets
with a focus on Sub-Saharan Africa. The partnership
underscores Japan’s continued leadership in leveraging
innovative financing solutions through the World
Bank Group Guarantee Platform to crowd in private
investment where it is most needed and where risks
remain highest.
GUARANTEEING FINANCIAL

DE-RISKING THROUGH GUARANTEES
MIGA completes the World Bank Group’s integrated
approach by using trust funds to provide guarantee
instruments that de-risk investments for both public
and private sector projects. Trust funds, including the
Renewable Energy Catalyst Trust Fund, the West Bank
and Gaza Trust Fund, and the Support for Ukraine’s
Reconstruction and Economy Trust Fund, share
guarantee exposure on individual projects via first-loss
layers and reinsurance. These instruments enable MIGA
to bridge the World Bank’s public sector work and IFC’s
private sector investments by guaranteeing higher-risk
projects and increasing investor confidence, particularly
in fragile and conflict-affected settings, while advancing
job creation and women’s economic empowerment.
The Fund for Advancing Sustainability complements
these efforts by strengthening environmental, social,
and gender practices and broadening access to
guarantees for small businesses in low-income
and fragile countries.

Over the past several years, IFC has been shifting
its model to not only deploy its own capital but to
mobilize more private capital from partners. That
shift is reflected in our fiscal 2026 results. The World
Bank Group mobilized $112 billion in private capital
in fiscal 2026, more than tripling from $35 billion in
fiscal 2022. IFC contributes to that outcome through
a range of instruments and products — guarantees,
originate-to-distribute structures, catalytic equity,
syndications, anchor investments, transaction
advisory, and local-currency financing — each designed
to address specific barriers that have historically
constrained private investment in developing
economies. In fiscal 2026, IFC achieved a record

AND JOBS
The World Bank Group is adapting to meet the scale
of the jobs challenge, shifting from a provider of
finance to a platform that channels global capital
flows into developing countries. Rather than
relying principally on our balance sheets, we are
increasingly using financing, guarantees, data, and
our convening role to crowd private capital into the
most productive sectors for job creation. This means
building investable pipelines, creating mechanisms
that allow risk to be distributed across a broader
set of investors, and connecting a much larger pool
of global capital to development opportunities.
In fiscal 2026, we made real progress and changes that
are already translating into results. While financing
from the World Bank Group’s own resources rose from
$98 billion to $123.5 billion over the last five years,
private capital mobilization surged from $35 billion in
fiscal 2022 to $112 billion in fiscal 2026.

The World Bank Group is also promoting private sector resilience in Ukraine. IBRD is
supporting policy reforms across several economic sectors and helping to keep basic
services for firms and citizens, while IFC has established risk-sharing facilities with
Ukrainian financial institutions to support on-lending to micro, small, and medium
enterprises; mobilized private sector participation in infrastructure, including telecom
and energy; supported businesses to safeguard jobs and food security; and backed
innovation and high-tech ventures through venture capital and private equity funds
to retain talent and build future growth. For its part, MIGA has extended and increased
guarantees to free up capital linked to two banks’ mandatory reserves, issuing
$448 million in new guarantees since February 2022 to keep small businesses
afloat and maintain employment opportunities.

WORLD BANK GROUP INITIATIVES
Our focus on job creation requires us to enhance our
external partnerships to generate new ideas. In fiscal
2026, the World Bank Group and partners launched a
new Mission 300 Private Sector Council to mobilize
the billions in private investment needed to connect
300 million Africans to electricity by 2030, and unlock
job creation across the continent. The Council,
comprising 14 leaders from diverse sectors, will help
drive strategies to accelerate commercial investment
that supports both energy access and employment.
Three years ago, the World Bank Group launched the
Private Sector Investment Lab to identify what was
holding back private investment in emerging markets.
Building on its work, we created the High-Level
Advisory Council on Jobs in 2024 to develop actionable
strategies for large-scale job creation. Both groups
brought together leaders from finance, business, and
government to provide new, outside-in thinking.

In our own supply chain, we leverage the World Bank
Group’s purchasing power through a category-based
approach to maximize efficiency and value, including
by focusing on job creation through small businesses
and local sourcing. We also keep operations running
smoothly by identifying and addressing risks from
approximately 22,000 vendors globally.
FUNDSCHAIN
The World Bank Group is the first multilateral
development bank to deploy a blockchain-based
platform for traceability of funds at the country level,
strengthening transparency and accountability in
fiduciary management. This initiative aligns with
the World Bank Group’s broader commitments to
digitalization and operational efficiency.

We also assess and track the development impact
of the advisory services that we provide to our
clients to help them adopt modern technologies
and management practices in various areas. In fiscal
2026, 60 percent of our completed advisory projects
implemented with client companies were found to
be mostly successful or better, below IFC’s target of
65 percent and the success rate in fiscal 2025. The
decline is driven primarily by project-specific design
and implementation issues, deliberate portfolio
clean-up efforts, and external disruptions that were
largely outside project control and created significant
implementation challenges across multiple business
lines and geographies.
